name: Liuyang Cheng
bio:
I study how the mechanics of soft materials can be used to create motion. My research focuses on twisted and coiled polymer actuators, nonlinear elasticity, and the design and control of artificial muscles.

I combine mechanical modeling with experiments to understand these materials and explore their use in soft robotic systems.

sections.title: Research & demos
sections.intro: How can a material be compliant during motion, yet resist excessive deformation? These animated mechanisms explore the ideas in my work on tensile J-curve materials and artificial ligaments.

items.title: Compliant motion, protective resistance
items.text: Two tensile ligaments pull in opposite directions. As the middle block moves, one stretches while the other relaxes. Their J-shaped response leaves a compliant central region and increasingly resists larger displacements. Adjust pre-stretch to explore the trade-off between stiffness and motion range.

items.title: From tensile ligaments to a tunable joint
items.text: The same principle extends to rotation. Opposing ligaments create a restoring torque about a pivot; pre-stretch changes the joint’s response. The animation connects joint angle, ligament tension, and resistance throughout the movement.

items.title: A tunable spring for a running leg
items.text: In the paper’s conceptual running model, a passive spring and an active linear actuator act in parallel. The actuator supplies the difference between the target leg force and the spring force. Explore how passive tuning changes that balance through compression, rebound, and flight.

items.title: From fiber geometry to muscle-like motion
items.text: Twisting and coiling turn a polymer fiber into a contractile actuator. I am interested in how geometry, stored energy, and material response work together to produce useful motion.

items.title: Artificial muscles in a moving light array
items.text: An ongoing exploration of coordinated TCPA motion for an art lighting system, including cycle stability, motion tracking, and control across a 32-actuator array.
